subject: Concurrency qualification & ratecap proposal for Acme Payments
messages:
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
To: Elena Ruiz <elena.ruiz@acme-payments.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-12-15T16:12:00-08:00
Subject: Concurrency qualification & ratecap proposal for Acme Payments

Elena — thanks again for the time earlier. Quick recap + a few follow-ups so we can scope the PoC and surface any rate-limit implications for procurement.

Call summary (as I heard it)
- Target tail latency: p95 <= 200ms for single-turn generation (non-streaming).
- Expected steady throughput: ~600 req/s (aggregated across 3 microservices).
- Peak/burst: up to ~900 req/s sustained for ~30-60s during campaign spikes.
- Max concurrent in-flight requests per service: ~500.
- Streaming: yes for chat flow — chunked token streaming expected, average stream length ~8 chunks, initial-response hardness matters (client-side timeout ~250ms).
- Connections: our services use connection pooling via HTTP/2 with keep-alive; typical connection count per host ~50 but we can increase.

Questions we need clarified before engineering deep-dive:
1) Are the 600 req/s steady-state requests equivalent-weight? i.e., similar token lengths/prompt complexity?
2) What client-side timeouts do you enforce (250ms noted) and how tolerant are clients to retries/backoff?
3) Do you require per-customer isolation (dedicated capacity) or is logical tenancy acceptable for the PoC?

Next steps I propose:
- Ben to propose a pragmatic ratecap + reserved concurrency profile we can commit to for the PoC.
- Run a 2-day performance baseline with a small Redwood dedicated pool (we can provision a pilot pool) to validate p95 and streaming behavior.
- Exchange the short attachment (I attached a one-tab workbook for you to fill gaps on token length and distribution).

Attachments: acme-concurrency-questions.xlsx (spreadsheet with traffic distribution + timeout fields)

If that matches your view I'll have Ben do a short technical note with suggested rate limit parameters and a draft SLO for the pilot.

Thanks,
Karthik
Account Executive — Redwood Inference

From: Elena Ruiz <elena.ruiz@acme-payments.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
Cc: ops@acme-payments.com
Date: 2027-12-15T18:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Concurrency qualification & ratecap proposal for Acme Payments

Karthik — thank you, that recap is accurate. A few clarifications and answers inline:

- Steady-state mix: roughly 70% short prompts (<=32 tokens), 25% medium (32-128), 5% long (>128). Short prompts are latency-sensitive (UI).
- Client timeouts: frontend enforces 250ms for first-token in UI flows, but we can extend to 500ms for server-side retries.
- Isolation: for now logical tenancy is fine for the PoC; enterprise procurement will want options for a dedicated pool long term.

One more ask: how do you handle connection pooling + long-lived streaming sockets at scale? We worry about socket exhaustion when many parallel streams open. I've attached our traffic snapshot (very small).

Attachment: acme-traffic-snapshot.csv

We can do the engineering deep-dive next Wed (our side) — are you available?

Best,
Elena Ruiz
Senior Platform Engineer — Acme Payments

From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>
To: Elena Ruiz <elena.ruiz@acme-payments.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-12-15T20:10:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Concurrency qualification & ratecap proposal for Acme Payments

Elena — quick technical note and a proposed PoC configuration based on Karthik's summary and your traffic mix:

Key assumptions we used
- Token distribution as noted (70/25/5). Average tokens per request ~45.
- Streaming sessions maintain a persistent HTTP/2 stream until conversation end; average active stream duration ~6s.
- Backend can open up to 250 connections from your cluster; we recommend multiplexing many logical requests over fewer physical connections where possible.

Redwood recommended pilot profile
- Reserved concurrency (steady): 600 concurrent request slots across the model pool.
- Burst headroom: +50% burst allowance (900 concurrent) with a 60s token-bucket window to absorb spikes.
- Per-client connection cap: 200 concurrent streams per client IP/credential to reduce head-of-line risk.
- Idle websocket/window timeout: 120s default, can be reduced to 60s if socket counts are high.
- Streaming throughput: we prioritize first-token generation for streaming; request-level p95 target remains <=200ms; streaming chunk p95 target <=120ms after first token.
- Rate limits: soft per-second limit of 600 req/s with graceful 429-based backoff that supports Retry-After and jittered exponential backoff.

Operational controls we recommend for the PoC
- Enable prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts to reduce token cost.
- Instrument retried requests vs initial requests; measure effective QPS after retries.
- Expose per-route token and request metrics to your telemetry (we can pipe to your Datadog).

Proof-of-concept plan
1) Week 0: Provision a small dedicated pool for Acme (1–2 GPUs) and baseline with your traffic snapshot.
2) Week 1: Run ramp tests to confirm p95 targets at 600 steady and 900 burst.
3) Week 2: Failure/injection testing (node loss, increased latency) and measure graceful fallback behavior.

Deliverables: Redwood will send a short PDF with the exact ratecap policy, a DocuSign for the PoC addendum if needed, and a small checklist for your infra team.

Attachments: redwood-ratecap-proposal.pdf

Happy to walk through these configs on a call — Karthik, I'll sync with you and schedule the deep-dive for Wed.

Thanks,
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
